title: Conjecture

label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
Let $G$ be a subcubic graph satisfying
$\Delta\bigl(G[V_3]\bigr)\le 1.$
Then
$\chi'_{\mathrm{rn}}(G)\le 5.$
head: environment

label: lem:hereditary
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:hereditary}
Let $G$ be a subcubic graph satisfying
$\Delta\bigl(G[V_3(G)]\bigr)\le 1.$
Then every subgraph $H$ of $G$ satisfies
$\Delta\bigl(H[V_3(H)]\bigr)\le 1.$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $v\in V_3(H)$, then
$3=d_H(v)\le d_G(v)\le 3,$
so $v\in V_3(G)$. Hence
$V_3(H)\subseteq V_3(G)$ and $H[V_3(H)]\subseteq G[V_3(G)].$
The assertion follows.
head: environment

label: lem:trees-cycles
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:trees-cycles}
Every subcubic tree or cycle admits a strong $5$-edge-coloring.
head: environment

label: lem:path-sequence
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $c_1=a$ and $c_\ell=b$. First choose
$c_2,\ldots,c_{\ell-3}$ successively, whenever this sequence is
nonempty, so that each $c_i$ avoids the already defined colors among
$c_{i-1}$ and $c_{i-2}$. Next choose $c_{\ell-2}$ and
$c_{\ell-1}$ successively, requiring each $c_i$ to avoid the already
defined colors among
$c_{i-1}, c_{i-2}, b.$
At most three colors are forbidden at every step, so all choices can
be made from $[5]$. The resulting sequence satisfies
$c_i\ne c_j$ whenever $0<|i-j|\le 2.$
Thus $\psi(e_i)=c_i$ defines the required strong edge-coloring.
head: environment

label: lem:bridge
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:bridge}
Every bridge of $G$ is a pendant edge.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $e=uv$ is a nonpendant bridge. Let $C_u$ and $C_v$ be
the components of $G-e$ containing $u$ and $v$, respectively. Since
$e$ is not pendant, both components contain an edge. Set
\[
  G_u=G\bigl[V(C_u)\cup\{v\}\bigr],
  \qquad
  G_v=G\bigl[V(C_v)\cup\{u\}\bigr].
\]
Both $G_u$ and $G_v$ are proper subgraphs of $G$ with fewer edges.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:hereditary} and the minimality of $G$, they admit
rich-neighbor $5$-edge-colorings $\varphi_u$ and $\varphi_v$. After
permuting the colors in $\varphi_v$, we may assume that
$\varphi_u(e)=\varphi_v(e)=\alpha.$

For a vertex $x$ of a graph $H$, let $E_H(x)$ denote the set of edges
of $H$ incident with $x$. Put
\[
  A_u=\varphi_u\bigl(E_{G_u}(u)\setminus\{e\}\bigr),
  \qquad
  A_v=\varphi_v\bigl(E_{G_v}(v)\setminus\{e\}\bigr).
\]
Properness and subcubicity give
$A_u,A_v\subseteq[5]\setminus\{\alpha\},$ $|A_u|,|A_v|\le 2.$
Since $[5]\setminus\{\alpha\}$ has four elements, there is a
permutation $\sigma$ of $[5]$ fixing $\alpha$ such that
$A_u\cap\sigma(A_v)=\varnothing.$
Replace $\varphi_v$ by $\sigma\circ\varphi_v$. The two colorings now agree
on $e$ and combine into a proper $5$-edge-coloring $\varphi$ of $G$.

For every $f\in E(G_u)\setminus\{e\}$,
$N_G(f)=N_{G_u}(f),$
so $f$ is rich under $\varphi$ if and only if it is rich under $\varphi_u$.
The analogous statement holds on the $v$-side, since permuting colors
preserves richness. Moreover,
$\varphi\bigl(N_G(e)\bigr)=A_u\cup\sigma(A_v).$
The colors in this union are pairwise distinct, and hence $e$ is
rich under $\varphi$.

Let $f\ne e$ be a non-isolated edge of $G$. In its side coloring,
$f$ has a rich neighbor. If that neighbor is not $e$, it remains rich
under $\varphi$; if it is $e$, then it is rich by the preceding
paragraph. Thus every non-isolated edge other than $e$ has a rich
neighbor.

Finally, since $C_u$ contains an edge, $e$ is non-isolated in $G_u$.
It therefore has a rich neighbor
$g\in E(G_u)\setminus\{e\}$ under $\varphi_u$. The edge $g$ remains rich
under $\varphi$, so $e$ also has a rich neighbor. Consequently, $\varphi$
is a rich-neighbor $5$-edge-coloring of $G$, a contradiction.
head: environment

label: cor:leaf-support
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:leaf-support}
If $x$ is a leaf of $G$ with neighbor $v$, then $d_G(v)=3$, and $x$ is the unique leaf neighbor of $v$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $G$ is connected and has more than one edge, $d_G(v)\ge2$. Suppose that either $d_G(v)=2$ or $v$ has another leaf neighbor. Then $v$ has a neighbor $w$ such that every neighbor of $v$ other
than $w$ is a leaf. Consequently, $vw$ lies on no cycle and is therefore a bridge.

If $w$ is a leaf, then every neighbor of $v$ is a leaf, so the connected graph $G$ is a star and hence a tree, a contradiction. Otherwise, $vw$ is a nonpendant bridge, contradicting Lemma~\ref{lem:bridge}. Therefore $d_G(v)=3$, and $x$ is the unique leaf neighbor of $v$.
head: environment

label: cl:K-core
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{cl:K-core}
The graph \(\hat G\) is connected and bridgeless, with
\(\delta(\hat G)\ge2\). If \(|V(\hat G)|\ge3\), then \(\hat G\) is
\(2\)-connected.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every vertex of \(\hat G\) has degree two or three in \(G\). By
Corollary~\ref{cor:leaf-support}, a \(2\)-vertex has no leaf neighbor
and a \(3\)-vertex has at most one. Hence
\(\delta(\hat G)\ge2\). Moreover, no leaf can be an internal vertex
of a path, so the connectivity of \(G\) implies that of \(\hat G\).

If \(ab\) were a bridge of \(\hat G\), then any \(a\)-\(b\) path in
\(G-ab\) would lie in \(\hat G\), a contradiction. Thus \(ab\) would
also be a bridge of \(G\). Since
\(d_G(a),d_G(b)\ge2\), this bridge would not be pendant, contrary to
Lemma~\ref{lem:bridge}. Therefore \(\hat G\) is bridgeless.

Finally, suppose that \(|V(\hat G)|\ge3\) and \(v\) is a cut vertex of
\(\hat G\). Each component of \(\hat G-v\) is joined to \(v\). Since
\(d_{\hat G}(v)\le3\) and \(\hat G-v\) has at least two components,
one of them is joined to \(v\) by exactly one edge. This edge is a
bridge of \(\hat G\), a contradiction. Hence \(\hat G\) is
\(2\)-connected.
head: environment

label: cl:B-at-least-two
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{cl:B-at-least-two}
$|V_3(G)|\ge2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $V_3(G)=\varnothing$, then the connected graph $G$ has maximum degree at most two. Since $G$ contains a cycle, it must itself be a cycle, contradicting Lemma~\ref{lem:trees-cycles}.

Suppose that $V_3(G)=\{v\}$. Every vertex of $\hat G$ other than $v$ has degree two in $\hat G$. By the handshaking lemma, $d_{\hat G}(v)$ is even. Since $2\le d_{\hat G}(v)\le3,$ we have $d_{\hat G}(v)=2$. Thus $\hat G$ is a connected $2$-regular graph and hence a cycle. Corollary~\ref{cor:leaf-support} now implies that $G$ is obtained from $\hat G$ by attaching exactly one pendant edge $g$ at $v$.

Let \(\varphi\) be a strong \(5\)-edge-coloring of \(\hat G\). Let
\(e,e'\) be the cycle edges incident with \(v\), and let \(f,f'\) be
their other cycle neighbors, where \(f=f'\) if \(\hat G\) is a
triangle. Choose
\(
\beta\in[5]\setminus
 \{\varphi(e),\varphi(e'),\varphi(f),\varphi(f')\}
\)
and set \(\varphi(g)=\beta\). The extension is proper, and the choice
of \(\beta\) ensures that \(e\) and \(e'\) remain rich. The
neighborhood of every other cycle edge is unchanged, so all cycle
edges remain rich. Hence every edge of \(G\) has a rich neighbor, a
contradiction.
head: environment

label: lem:star-forest
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the minimality of $F$, every edge $xy\in F$ has an
endpoint of degree one in $G'_F$; otherwise, both $x$ and $y$ would
remain covered after deleting $xy$, and $F-\{xy\}$ would still be an
edge cover of $G'$. In particular, $F$ contains no parallel edges,
since the endpoints of two parallel edges would both have degree at
least two in $G'_F$.

Let $C$ be a component of $G'_F$. If $C\cong K_2$, then $C$ is a
star. Otherwise, choose a vertex $x\in V(C)$ with $d_C(x)\ge2$.
Every neighbor of $x$ has degree one in $C$. Since $C$ is connected,
every edge of $C$ is incident with $x$. Hence $C$ is a star.
head: environment

label: lem:selected-rich
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:selected-rich}
Suppose that all remaining uncolored edges incident with each
\(v\in B\) are assigned pairwise distinct colors from \(\Lambda(v)\).
Then the resulting partial coloring is proper at every vertex of
\(B\), and the colors on \(N_G(e)\) are pairwise distinct for every
edge \(e\) of a selected thread. Consequently, every selected-thread
edge is rich in every proper edge-coloring of \(G\) extending this
partial coloring.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First consider the center \(z\) of a star component of \(G'_F\).
The selected first edges incident with \(z\) have the distinct colors
\(1,\ldots,t\), whereas the newly colored edges incident with \(z\)
receive pairwise distinct colors from
\(
\Lambda(z)
=[5]\setminus\bigl(\{1,\ldots,t\}\cup\{4\}\bigr).
\)
Thus the coloring is proper at \(z\).

For each \(i\in[t]\), the neighbors of \(e^i_1\) are \(e^i_2\), which
has color \(4\), and the other edges incident with \(z\). Their colors
belong to the pairwise disjoint sets
\(
\{4\},
\{1,\ldots,t\}\setminus\{i\},
\Lambda(z),
\)
and are pairwise distinct within each set. Hence all neighbors of
\(e^i_1\) have distinct colors.

Now consider a leaf \(z_i\). The two other edges incident with \(z_i\)
receive distinct colors from
\(
\Lambda(z_i)=[5]\setminus\{a_i,b_i\},
\)
where
\(
a_i=\varphi(e^i_{\ell_i-1})
\)
and
\(
b_i=\varphi(e^i_{\ell_i}).
\)
Since these colors avoid \(b_i\), the coloring is proper at \(z_i\).
Since they also avoid \(a_i\), all neighbors of
\(e^i_{\ell_i}\) have pairwise distinct colors.

Finally, let \(e^i_j\) be an internal edge of \(P_i\), where
\(2\le j\le\ell_i-1\). Its endpoints lie in \(\hat G-B\) and hence
are \(2\)-vertices of \(G\). Therefore
\(
N_G(e^i_j)=\{e^i_{j-1},e^i_{j+1}\}.
\)
These two edges have distinct colors by
\eqref{eq:periodic-pattern1}.

Thus every neighbor of a selected-thread edge has already been colored,
and these colors are pairwise distinct. They are unchanged by any
further extension, so every selected-thread edge is rich in every
proper extension.
head: environment

label: lem:sub2-list
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sub2-list}
Let \(H\) be a graph with \(\Delta(H)\le2\), and let \(L\) assign a
list of colors to each edge of \(H\). Suppose that \(|L(e)|\ge2\) for
every \(e\in E(H)\), and that every cycle component of \(H\) contains
an edge \(e\) with \(|L(e)|\ge3\). Then \(H\) has a proper
edge-coloring \(\psi\) such that
\(
\psi(e)\in L(e)
\)
for every 
\(
e\in E(H).
\)
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every component of \(H\) containing an edge is a path or a cycle.
A path can be colored greedily from one end, since each edge has at
most one previously colored neighbor and a list of size at least two.

For a cycle component \(C\), choose \(e_0\in E(C)\) with
\(|L(e_0)|\ge3\). Color the path \(C-e_0\) greedily. The edge \(e_0\)
then has at most two colored neighbors, so a color in \(L(e_0)\)
distinct from their colors remains available. Coloring the components
independently completes the proof.
head: environment

label: lem:port-list1
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let
\(
S=\{e\in E(Q):|L(e)|=1\}.
\)
Suppose that \(e\) has a unique endpoint \(v\) in \(B\). By
\eqref{eq:port-data} and \(d_Q(v)=3-d_F(v)\),
\(
|L(e)|=|\Lambda(v)|
       =4-d_F(v)
       =1+d_Q(v)
       \ge2.
\)
Thus every edge of \(S\) has both endpoints in \(B\) and hence
corresponds to an unselected \(B\)-thread of length one. Since every
list contains \(5\), we have \(L(e)=\{5\}\) for each \(e\in S\).
Moreover, \(S\) is a matching by~\eqref{eq:M-matching1}.

Color every edge of \(S\) with \(5\), let \(Q'=Q-S\), and define, for
each \(e\in E(Q')\),
\[
L'(e)=
\begin{cases}
L(e)\setminus\{5\},
   & \text{if \(e\) is adjacent to an edge of \(S\)},\\
L(e),
   & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

We first show that
\(
|L'(e)|\ge2
\)
for every 
\(
e\in E(Q').
\)
If both endpoints of \(e\) lie in \(B\), then \(e\) corresponds to a length-one thread. Since all such edges form a matching, \(e\) is not adjacent to \(S\). Hence \(L'(e)=L(e)\), and \(|L'(e)|\ge2\) because
\(e\notin S\). Now suppose that \(e\) has a unique endpoint \(v\) in \(B\). If no edge of \(S\) is incident with \(v\), then \(L'(e)=L(e)\), and the equality above gives \(|L'(e)|\ge2\). Otherwise, \(e\) and an edge of
\(S\) are both incident with \(v\). Since \(d_Q(v)\le2\), we have \(d_Q(v)=2\), and therefore
\(
|L(e)|=1+d_Q(v)=3.
\)
Deleting \(5\) leaves \(|L'(e)|=2\).

It remains to verify the condition on cycle components. Let \(C\) be
a cycle component of \(Q'\). No edge arising from a pendant edge or
from a thread of length at least three can lie on \(C\), since such an
edge has a degree-one endpoint in \(Q\). Thus every edge of \(C\)
either corresponds to a length-one thread or belongs to a retained
length-two thread. Since the length-one edges form a matching, \(C\)
contains an edge \(e\) from a length-two thread.

Let \(v\in B\) be the endpoint of \(e\) in \(B\). Since \(v\) lies on
the cycle \(C\),
\(
d_{Q'}(v)=2.
\)
As \(d_Q(v)\le2\), it follows that \(d_Q(v)=2\), and no edge of \(S\)
is incident with \(v\). The other endpoint of \(e\) lies outside
\(B\), whereas every edge of \(S\) has both endpoints in \(B\).
Hence \(e\) is not adjacent to \(S\), and
\(
|L'(e)|=|L(e)|=1+d_Q(v)=3.
\)
Therefore every cycle component of \(Q'\) contains an edge whose list
has size at least three.

Since \(\Delta(Q')\le2\), Lemma~\ref{lem:sub2-list} gives a proper
\(L'\)-edge-coloring of \(Q'\). Together with the edges of \(S\), all
colored \(5\), this yields a proper edge-coloring \(\psi\) of \(Q\):
the edges of \(S\) form a matching, and \(5\) was deleted from the
lists of all edges adjacent to \(S\). Finally,
\(L'(e)\subseteq L(e)\) for every \(e\in E(Q')\), so
\(\psi(e)\in L(e)\) for every \(e\in E(Q)\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The preceding construction yields a proper \(5\)-edge-coloring
\(\varphi\) of \(G\). Properness at vertices of \(B\) follows from
Lemmas~\ref{lem:port-list1} and~\ref{lem:selected-rich}. At the
internal vertices of selected threads it follows from the periodic
pattern~\eqref{eq:periodic-pattern1}; for unselected threads it follows
from the proper coloring of \(Q\) when the length is two, from
\eqref{eq:length-three} when the length is three, and from
Lemma~\ref{lem:path-sequence} when the length is at least four.
Properness at leaves is immediate.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:selected-rich}, every selected-thread edge is rich.
Since each selected thread has length at least two by
\eqref{eq:selected-long}, every such edge is adjacent to another rich
edge on the same thread.

Because \(F\) covers \(B\), every vertex of \(B\) is incident with a
selected thread. Hence every pendant edge and every edge of an
unselected thread incident with \(B\) has a rich selected-thread
neighbor. This covers all edges of unselected threads of length at
most two and the end edges of all longer unselected threads.

For an unselected thread of length three, its middle edge is adjacent
to the first end edge, which is rich by the choice in
\eqref{eq:length-three}. For an unselected thread of length at least
four, all internal edges are rich, and there are at least two
consecutive internal edges. Thus every internal edge has a rich
internal neighbor.

Consequently, every non-isolated edge of \(G\) has a rich neighbor.
Therefore \(\varphi\) is a rich-neighbor \(5\)-edge-coloring of \(G\),
contradicting the choice of \(G\).
head: environment
